newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian newspapers hail China-India agreement.
newsitem.headline: Indian newspapers hail China-India agreement.

text.p: Indian newspapers on Saturday hailed an agreement between India and neighbouring China aimed at reducing tensions along their rugged Himalayan border.
India and China on Friday signed an agreement on confidence- building measures in military areas which could lead to troop and weapon cutbacks.
It was signed on the second day of a state visit by Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who travels on Sunday to Pakistan, India's traditional rival.
The Times of India daily said the world's two most populous countries pledged to work towards "a long-term enduring relationship".
It described the agreement as "a virtual no war pact".
It was signed by Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen after talks between Jiang Zemin and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
"India and China added real substance... to their joint agenda of peace by committing themselves against use of military capability against each other," the Hindustan Times daily said:
The Times of India said: "For the first time, the countries spoke formally of a mutual reduction in military and paramilitary strength along the line of actual control."
But Rasheed Talib, an independent political commentator, told Reuters: "In 1995 there was a small area of agreement. I see that being consolidated."
"The recent agreement is a step towards the goal that is still quite distant," he said.
India and China signed an agreement in 1993 to ease tension along their frontier during a visit by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to Beijing.
In August 1995, India and China agreed to pull back their troops from four border posts in India's northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, parts of which are claimed by China.

The two sides on Friday also signed pacts on preventing illegal drug trafficking, shipping links and an Indian consular office in Hong Kong after mid-1997 when China resumes sovereignty of the territory.
But they failed to sign a planned investment guarantee because of technical difficulties, officials said.
